# ZurfurGui Documentation (User Guide)
> Minimal, inheritance-free C# WebAssembly & Desktop GUI framework using Model Data View (MDV) and JSON5.

================================================================================
FILE: docs/architecture.md
================================================================================
# Architecture

## Overview

This repo experiments with a minimal C# GUI stack (WebAssembly + native Windows) using
a **Model Data View (MDV)** approach. This document describes the design direction and the shape of
the system. Details live in the documents listed under [Documentation map](#documentation-map).

## Design direction (MDV)

Goal: replace **MVVM** style runtime bindings with **generated, compile-time view data shapes**.

- The **View (V)** declares the **data (D)** it needs (in ZUI JSON `$data` section).
- Code generation produces:
  - Code-behind partial controller class (`*.zui` → `<ViewName>.Control.g.cs`)
  - A strongly typed data class (`*.zui` → `<ViewName>.Data.g.cs`)
  - Library initialization `ZurfurMain.cs` partial class, constructed from `*.zui` and `*.zth` files.
- You can:
  - use the generated data class as-is (for example, deserialize or populate it directly), or
  - extend it as a `partial` class to map to/from the domain **model (M)**.
- Avoid runtime reflection for MDV/data propagation and bindings. Prefer code generation (or other
  compile-time mechanisms) so updates are strongly typed, AOT-friendly, and trimming-safe.

## Terminology

- **Model (M):** domain logic/types; should remain UI-agnostic when practical.
- **Data (D):** view-shaped data generated from the view's declared needs.
- **View (V):** the renderer/layout/input layer that consumes the generated data class.

## Two-tree architecture

MDV keeps the **control tree** and the **data graph** independent:

- **Control tree:** the hierarchy of views and controls.
   - Each control has a `View` that owns its layout, draw, and input handlers.
   - Each control has a `DataContext` that is a concrete instance of the generated data class.
- **Data graph:** the data objects that supply values to the views.
   - Never reference controls or views.
   - May include references to sub-control `DataContext` objects
   - May optionally be used as the DTO, or may include user conversions to/from the model. 

**Key principle:** Controls reference data; data may reference other data objects—but **data never
references controls**. The control tree and data graph are independent; the data graph shape is
determined by what the view declares in `$data`.

The generated controller and its generated data type are intentionally related: a view-specific
controller consuming a view-specific data shape is the MDV relationship. The required decoupling is
between data and controls, not between a controller and the data contract it renders.

### Relation to MVVM

This resembles MVVM's visual tree plus ViewModel graph, but MDV does not assume a 1:1 tree shape. The
data side should not reach into controls; integration should happen through declared bindings.

## Visibility and the platform boundary

Application code should use the GUI API. The operating-system and browser integration is an
implementation detail behind the platform boundary.

# Initialization Procedure

This document describes startup and initialization for applications using ZurfurGui, including
Windows and browser targets.

## Overview


The source generator emits a `ZurfurMain.InitializeControls()` method for each project containing
ZUI or theme files. It registers control types, concrete data-controller factories, closed generic
control usages, property keys, and themes. Each project must declare a `static partial class
ZurfurMain` (the generator reports `ZUI005` otherwise). See [Code generation](code-generation.md)
for details.

## Startup Sequence

1. **Application entry point**
   - The application starts in its own `Program.Main` or equivalent entry point.

2. **Platform startup**
   - The application calls the platform-specific entry point:
     - **Windows:** `WinStart.Start(userCallback)`
     - **Browser:** `BrowserStart.Start(canvasId, userCallback)`
   - The callback receives the created `AppWindow`. `Loader.Init` calls
     `ZurfurMain.MainApp()` before invoking this callback.

3. **Library initialization**
   - `WinStart.Start` or `BrowserStart.Start` calls `Loader.Init(...)`.
   - `Loader.Init` initializes built-in layouts, calls the application's `ZurfurMain.MainApp()`,
     creates an `AppWindow`, and finally invokes the platform callback with that window.

4. **Generated registration**
   - `ZurfurMain.MainApp()` must call the generated `InitializeControls()` method before creating
     controls.
   - The generated method:
     - runs static constructors for property registration, including open generic controls;
     - registers ordinary controls for creation from ZUI controller names;
     - registers open generic controls (e.g. `ComboBox<>`) under their bare class name, so closed
       usages can be resolved later by name;
     - registers concrete data types to controller factories;
     - registers closed generic controller usages discovered in ZUI files, resolving the base
       generic control and item controller by bare name at runtime (see
       [Loader registration and lookup](#loader-registration-and-lookup)); and
     - registers themes.
   - If using third-party libraries or plugins, call their `ZurfurMain.InitializeControls()` methods
     at this stage too, before any of your own closed generic usages of their controls are
     registered or loaded.

5. **Application logic**
   - After all required initialization methods return, the callback can create windows and controls,
     populate concrete data objects, and set the main application window.

## Example startup code

`Loader.Init` invokes `ZurfurMain.MainApp()` for library and generated registration. The platform
callback is separate and receives the `AppWindow` used to set up the main application control.
For Windows:

```csharp
[STAThread]
static void Main()
{
    WinStart.Start(appWindow =>
    {
        appWindow.SetMainappWindow(new MyMainForm());
    });
}
```

The application's `ZurfurMain` class must be partial and call generated registration before
application logic:

```csharp
public static partial class ZurfurMain
{
    public static void MainApp()
    {
        InitializeControls();

        // Register controls and themes supplied by third-party libraries.
        // ThirdPartyDll.ZurfurMain.InitializeControls();
    }
}
```

For browser targets, pass the canvas id and an `AppWindow` callback:

```csharp
BrowserStart.Start("main", appWindow =>
{
    appWindow.SetMainappWindow(new MyMainForm());
});
```

## Loader and control initialization

### Loader registration and lookup

`Loader` keeps separate registries for controls and concrete data-item controllers:

- `RegisterControl` maps a controller name to a `Controllable` type and factory. ZUI controller
  lookup tries the fully qualified name, the containing control's namespace, its `$use` namespaces,
  and then `ZurfurGui.Controls`. A missing `$controller` resolves to `Panel`. Re-registering the
  same controller name with a different type throws.
  - Closed generic usages found in ZUI files are registered under their usage string. The generator
    resolves and emits those types directly; see [Code generation](code-generation.md).
- `RegisterDataController` maps a concrete data type to a factory. Lookup uses the exact runtime
  type; duplicate data-type registration throws. The factory receives and assigns the same data
  instance to the controller's `DataContext`.

Generated controllers load through the control registry. Data-item controller lookup occurs when a
data-driven control such as `ComboBox` creates an item controller. For generated registrations, see
[Code generation](code-generation.md).

## Control content loading

Controls load two kinds of content: template content is the control's own ZUI-defined visual
structure, while parent content is supplied by the containing control through the child control's
`$content`.

The loader and generated initialization call in this order:

```text
Control constructor (generated or hand-written)
        |
        v
Generated InitializeControl()
        |
        +--> View = new(this)
        |
        +--> ZuiRuntime.Load(control, control's own ZUI JSON)
                |
                +--> merge template properties and apply template layout to View
                |
                +--> add template content: create children and add their Views to View
                |
                +--> ApplyDataProperties recursively, children before parent
        |
        +--> cache named child controls
        |
        +--> create the control's default DataContext, if it has data bindings

Parent creates a child from its $content
        |
        v
Loader.CreateControl(child properties, context)
        |
        +--> resolve and invoke the child controller factory
        |       child constructor completes its own InitializeControl sequence
        |
        +--> merge parent-supplied instance properties onto the child's View
        |
        +--> apply parent-supplied layout to the child's ContentHost
        |
        +--> add parent content: create children and add their Views to ContentHost
```

`ContentHost` determines where parent-supplied content is placed, not the call order or content
ownership. It is `View` by default. Template content is control-owned structure, while parent content
is supplied by the parent.

For `DataContext` defaults and binding behavior, see [Property Binding](property-binding.md).

`ScrollViewer` uses the default template-loading behavior: its own ZUI content defines the clipped
viewport, content window, and overlay scrollbars. Its `ContentHost` is `_contentWindow`, so parent
content is routed separately from the scrollbars. `Window` uses the same pattern: its template
defines the title bar, clipped `_windowContent`, and resize handle, and its `ContentHost` routes
parent content to `_windowContent`. Its `title` data property forwards to the title `TextView`'s
`text` property.

This explicit distinction avoids inferring the loading phase from the current child count and
supports controls with templates or named content hosts without loader-specific phase detection.
For measurement, arrangement, sizing, and content-extent behavior, see
[ScrollViewer](scroll-viewer.md).

FILE: docs/zui-format.md
================================================================================
# ZUI and ZTH File Format

`.zui` files are Zurfur UI configuration files, and `.zth` files are Zurfur Theme configuration
files. Both use a small modified JSON5 format. This document describes the syntax and the reserved
keys. For what the generator does with these files, see [Code generation](code-generation.md). For
the `$data` section, see [Property binding](property-binding.md). For theme files, see
[Styles and themes](styles-and-themes.md).

## Syntax

The format is essentially JSON with comments, and dictionary keys do not need quotes. It is parsed
by `ZurfurGuiGen/Json.cs` in the generator and by `System.Text.Json` at runtime. In addition to
standard JSON, the generator parser supports these JSON5 features:

- **`//` line comments and `/* */` block comments** — a comment outside a string value is skipped.
- **Trailing commas** — a comma after the last property in an object or the last element in an
  array is silently accepted. This matches the JSONC convention used by `tsconfig.json`, VS Code
  `settings.json`, etc.
- **Unquoted dictionary keys** — ASCII identifier keys, including keys beginning with `$` and
  containing `.` or `-`, do not need quotes.
- **Single-quoted strings.**
- **Relaxed decimal numbers** — `+5`, `.5`, and `5.` are accepted.

Not supported: `NaN`, `Infinity`, hexadecimal numbers, the full Unicode identifier grammar, uncommon
JSON5 escape forms, and `null` values.

## Naming conventions

- Keys beginning with `$` are global symbols reserved by ZurfurGUI, such as `$controller`, `$name`,
  `$margin`, and `$width`.
- Type names are PascalCase (including built-in aliases like `Int`, `Bool`, `String`, etc.).
- Field names are camelCase.
- The source generator converts from JSON style to C# style when generating code. Field and property
  names become PascalCase in C#, and built-in type aliases are normalized to the corresponding C#
  keywords.

## Top-level keys of a `.zui` file

| Key | Required | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `$namespace` | Yes | The C# namespace of the generated controller and data classes. |
| `$controller` | Yes | The controller name, which must match the file name. May use the generic form `Name<T> where T : Constraint`. |
| `$use` | No | An array of strings naming extra namespaces searched when resolving child controller names. |
| `$implements` | No | A handwritten C# interface the generated data class implements, such as `IComboBoxItem`. |
| `$accessModifier` | No | The C# access modifier (`public` or `internal`) of the generated controller and data classes. Defaults to `public`. |
| `$data` | No | Declares the view's data shape. See [Property binding](property-binding.md). |
| `$content` | No | The array of child controls that make up the control's own template. |

`$use` must be an array of strings. A single string is an error.

Top-level `$data` entries whose names begin with `$` are only allowed in `Panel.zui`, which defines
the library's global `$`-prefixed properties.

## Comments in generated code

Comments are collected by the generator and emitted into generated code as XML doc comments where
appropriate:

- `//` line comments immediately preceding a `$data` property are emitted as `<summary>` XML doc
  comments on the members generated for that binding.
- A comment at the top of the file, before the top-level object, is emitted as the `<summary>` of
  the generated controller and data classes.

Generator-only metadata (`#comment`, `$namespace`, `$use`, `$data`, and `$accessModifier`) is removed
from the JSON before it is embedded in the generated controller, so it is not seen by the runtime
loader.

## `.zth` theme files

A `.zth` file uses the same syntax. Its top-level `name` key must be present and must match the
file name without its extension. Themes are registered by the generated
`ZurfurMain.InitializeControls()`. The token syntax is described in
[Styles and themes](styles-and-themes.md).

## Configuration preference

Prefer setting view properties (for example `$hitTest`, `$layout`, and styled values) in the `*.zui`
file rather than in code-behind. Declarative configuration can be overridden by parents and themes,
while constructor code cannot. Keep code-behind for behavior such as events and layout logic.

================================================================================
FILE: docs/code-generation.md
================================================================================
# Code Generation

## Overview

This repo uses a Roslyn incremental source generator (`src/ZurfurGuiGen/GenerateZui.cs`) to turn
ZUI and ZTH files into C#. The generator targets `netstandard2.0`, and the code it generates targets
`.NET 10`. For the file syntax, see [ZUI and ZTH file format](zui-format.md). For the `$data`
section and binding categories, see [Property binding](property-binding.md). For how the generated
registration code is used at startup, see [Initialization](initialization.md).

## File discovery

The generator processes `.zui` and `.zth` files included as project `AdditionalFiles`. In Visual
Studio, set the build action to `C# analyzer` / `AdditionalFiles`, or add the files in the project:

```xml
<ItemGroup>
	<AdditionalFiles Include="**\*.zui" />
	<AdditionalFiles Include="**\*.zth" />
</ItemGroup>
```

The project must also reference the generator as an analyzer:

```xml
<ProjectReference Include="..\ZurfurGuiGen\ZurfurGuiGen.csproj"
				  OutputItemType="Analyzer" ReferenceOutputAssembly="false" />
```

If the generator does not pick up a file, check its build action or the project's `AdditionalFiles`
items.

# Property Binding

## Overview

ZurfurGUI's property system connects application data, controls, and styles. A ZUI `$data` declaration
defines the values a control exposes and how they interact with its view and styles.

## The `$data` section

Declare data properties in a `.zui` file's `$data` section. Each entry specifies `type`, `bind`, and
optional `default` and `flags` values:

| Field | Required | Description | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `type` | Yes | The property type. Prefix with `?` for nullable types and `[]` for collections. | `Color`, `?string`, `[]Item` |
| `bind` | Yes | Controls whether the value is data-only, style-aware, style-only, view-only, attached, or forwarded. | `data`, `styledData`, `styled`, `property`, `attachedProperty`, `attachedStyle` |
| `default` | No | Initial value expressed as a C# expression. | `"100"`, `"Orientation.horizontal"`, `"new Color(128, 128, 128)"` |
| `flags` | No | Comma-separated `ViewFlags` used when the property changes. | `draw`, `measure`, `styleThis`, `styleDown` |

For example:

```
$data: {
    // Current application value; not mirrored to a view property.
    value: {
        type: "double",
        bind: "data"
    },
    // Initial orientation, with a style-aware view value.
    orientation: {
        type: "Orientation",
        bind: "styledData",
        default: "Orientation.horizontal"
    },
    // Themeable visual configuration that is not application data.
    thumbColor: {
        type: "Color",
        bind: "styled",
        default: "new Color(128, 128, 128)",
        flags: "draw"
    }
}
```

## Binding category summary

| `bind` value | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `data` | Application state stored in `DataContext`, not mirrored to the view. |
| `styledData` | A data value that can override a style-provided view value. |
| `styled` | Themeable view configuration that is not application data. |
| `property` | A view property read directly without style resolution. |
| `data:<target>` | A parent data value forwarded to a child control's data property. |
| `attachedProperty` | A non-style-aware view property that can be set on other controls. |
| `attachedStyle` | A style-aware view property that can be set on other controls. |

Use `DataContext` for `data`, forwarded values, and writes to `styledData`. Use `Properties` for
view-facing values, and read `styledData` through `Properties` to get its effective style value.
Setting nullable styled values to `null` removes the local override.

Collections use `[]Type` and must use `bind: "data"`. They cannot be nullable or forwarded. A generic
type parameter can be used by data and forwarded bindings, but not by bindings that generate
view-facing property keys.

FILE: docs/styles-and-themes.md
================================================================================
# Style and Theming System

## Overview

This document explains how theme tokens are declared, applied, and resolved.

ZurfurGui uses a **theme token system** where visual properties reference named tokens
defined in theme files. Theme tokens are resolved at runtime by walking up the view
hierarchy, allowing flexible theming at any level—from the entire application down to
individual controls.

The key components are:

- **Theme files** (`.zth`) define named tokens (color, spacing, fonts, etc.)
- **View files** (`.zui`) reference tokens using `"${token.name}"` syntax
- **Theme resolution** walks up the view chain searching for active themes
- **Token fallbacks** using the `|` operator enable third-party controls to gracefully
  degrade

## Theme Files (`.zth`)

`.zth` means Zurfur Theme. Theme files use the modified JSON5 syntax described in
[ZUI and ZTH File Format](zui-format.md). Each theme has a name and a dictionary of variables.

```
{
    name: "ZurfurDefault",
    variables: {
        color.surface.canvas: "#EAF4FB",
        color.text.primary: "#1F1F1F",
        spacing.medium: "8",
        radius.corner.medium: "4",
        color.interactive.primary.stroke: "isPressed ? #005A9E; isPointerOver ? #0078D4; #909090"
    }
}
```

### Token Features

**Conditional expressions**: Tokens can respond to view states using
`condition ? value; alternativeValue` syntax:

```
color.interactive.primary.background: "isPressed ? #A6D2F2; isPointerOver ? #D2E8FA; #C6E0F7",
color.scroll.thumb.background: "isPressed ? #005A9E; ScrollBar.isExpanded ? #6A9FD0; #8BB4DC80"
```

Supported conditions:
- `isPointerOver` / `!isPointerOver`
- `isPressed` / `!isPressed`
- Any registered boolean property using its exact name, such as `ScrollBar.isExpanded`
- A leading `!` negates any supported condition

Registered boolean property conditions read the control's current runtime value rather than resolving
the property as a style. Conditions must name a property exactly; unknown properties and non-boolean
properties are invalid conditions.

Multiple expressions are separated by semicolons, evaluated in order until a matching
condition is found. The last value (without a condition) serves as the default.

**Property merging**: Tokens can contain partial property specifications that merge
together using the `IMergable` interface. For example, spacing tokens can define
individual edges:

```
spacing.horizontal.medium: "left:8,right:8",
spacing.vertical.small: "top:4,bottom:4"
```

These merge when both are referenced via `|`, creating
`"left:8,right:8,top:4,bottom:4"`.

### Built-in Themes

ZurfurGui includes several base themes:

- **ZurfurBase**: Common tokens that rarely change (spacing, corner radii, stroke
  widths, default sizes)
- **ZurfurDefault**: Light theme with Fluent 2-inspired colors
- **ZurfurDefaultDark**: Dark variant
- **ZurfurCherry**: Alternative light theme
- **ZurfurCherryDark**: Alternative dark theme

`ZurfurBase` and `ZurfurDefault` act as ultimate fallbacks during token resolution (see
below).

## Using Theme Tokens in Views

In `.zui` files, wrap token names with `${}` to reference theme tokens:

```
{
    $controller: "Button",
    $borderWidth: "${stroke.width.default}",
    $borderRadius: "${radius.corner.medium}",
    $borderColor: "${color.interactive.primary.stroke}",
    $backgroundColor: "${color.interactive.primary.background}"
}
```

When a view requests a property, its token expression is resolved using the active themes.

### Token Fallback with `|`

Multiple token names can be specified with `|`. This is critical for third-party
controls that define their own tokens but want to fall back to standard system tokens if
the user's theme doesn't define the custom ones:

```
$padding: "${spacing.my-control-inner-padding | spacing.horizontal.small | spacing.vertical.extra-small}"
```

First, the custom token `spacing.my-control-inner-padding` is tried.  If the application has
supplied the token, it is taken.  If not, the next tokens are tried in order. If 
`spacing.horizontal.small` provides a partial value (e.g., only `left` and `right`), 
`spacing.vertical.extra-small` can complete it by providing `top` and `bottom`. If the first 
token fully resolves the property, the rest are ignored.

The `|` operator combined with `IMergable` properties enables powerful composition:

```
TextView.font: "${style.test.font.c1 | style.test.font.c2}"
```

If `font.c1` defines `size:28` and `font.c2` defines `name:Times New Roman`, the
resolved font has both size and name.

### Providing Defaults for `styled` Properties

For a control property declared with `bind: "styled"`, provide its value through the control's theme-token
mapping and include a fallback token that is defined by the built-in themes. This lets
consumers override a control-specific token without requiring every theme to define it. If the
optional token is absent, the fallback supplies a usable value:

```
{
    ScrollBar.thumbEdgeInset: "${size.scrollbar.thumb.edge-inset | spacing.extra-small}",
    $data: {
        thumbEdgeInset: {
            type: "Double",
            bind: "styled",
            flags: "render"
        }
    }
}
```

Here, `size.scrollbar.thumb.edge-inset` is an optional, control-specific token; `spacing.extra-small` is
the guaranteed fallback defined in `ZurfurBase`. The styled-only data item has no `default`: its
value comes from the token mapping. For every `styled` property, use this pattern rather than
putting a `default` on the data item. Choose a fallback with a compatible value type and ensure it
exists in a built-in theme, so the control works when the optional token is not defined.

This guidance is specific to `styled` properties. Keep `default` values on ordinary data, `styledData`,
or `property` bindings when they need an initial runtime value, such as a control's default orientation.

For the distinction between `styled` and `property` bindings, see
[Property Binding](property-binding.md).

## Selecting and Activating Themes

### Setting Application-Wide Themes

To set the theme for the entire application, use the top-level `View`'s `ActiveThemes`
property:

```csharp
view.ActiveThemes = ["MyCustomTheme", "ZurfurDefault"];
```

The first theme has highest priority. Theme resolution then falls back to `ZurfurDefault` and
`ZurfurBase`.

### Setting Themes on Subviews

You can set `ActiveThemes` on any `View` in the hierarchy to apply themes locally:

```csharp
myPanel.View.ActiveThemes = ["SpecialPanelTheme"];
```

Child controls will use this theme (and any themes further up the chain) when resolving
tokens.

## Resolution behavior

An explicitly set property takes precedence over a theme value. Otherwise, each token candidate is
searched through the view's active themes, its parent views, and the built-in fallbacks. Candidate
order takes precedence over theme priority: the first candidate is fully resolved before the next is
tried. Partial `IMergable` values can combine across themes and token candidates. If no candidate
provides a value, resolution fails.

## Creating Custom Themes

To create a custom theme:

1. **Create a `.zth` file** in your project (mark as AdditionalFiles).

2. **Define a unique name and variables**:

```
{
    name: "MyBrandTheme",
    variables: {
        color.surface.canvas: "#F0F0FF",
        color.text.primary: "#000033",
        my.custom.accent: "#FF6600"
    }
}
```

3. **Reference your tokens in `.zui` files**:

```
$backgroundColor: "${my.custom.accent | color.interactive.primary.background}"
```

The `|` fallback ensures your control still works in themes that don't define
`my.custom.accent`.

4. **Activate your theme** at runtime:

```csharp
appWindow.View.ActiveThemes = ["MyBrandTheme"];
```

FILE: docs/controls.md
================================================================================
# Controls

This guide gives a short introduction to the controls provided by ZurfurGui. Controls are declared in
ZUI JSON5 files and loaded into generated C# controller classes. A view with named controls gets fields
for those controls in its generated controller, and application behavior can be added in the matching
`.Control.cs` partial class.

For generated data and binding behavior, see [Property Binding](property-binding.md).

## Application setup

Applications call generated `InitializeControls` before creating controls. Use
`SetMainappWindow` for the main content and `ShowWindow` for additional windows. See
[Initialization](initialization.md) for the startup example.

## ZUI controls

### Panel

`Panel` is a general-purpose container. Use its `$content` section to contain other controls and use
`$layout` to arrange those controls. Common layouts include `Row`, `Column`, and `Dock`.

```
{
    $controller: "Panel",
    $layout: "Row",
    $content: [
        { $controller: "TextView", text: "Name:" },
        { $controller: "Button", text: "Edit" }
    ]
}
```

When no `$layout` is specified, `Panel` uses its default layout and arranges each child independently.
Set the qualified `"Panel.Offset"` property on a child to shift its layout position. Its positive right
and bottom edges contribute to the Panel's measured extent:

```
{
    $controller: "Panel",
    $content: [
        {
            $controller: "Window",
            Panel.Offset: "x:24,y:32"
        }
    ]
}
```

Negative offsets do not move the Panel's `(0, 0)` content origin and may place content outside its
measured bounds.
Custom layouts such as `Row`, `Column`, and `Dock` do not use `Panel.Offset`.

### Window

`Window` provides window chrome around parent-supplied content. Its template includes a title bar, close
control, and resize handle. Parent `$content` is placed in the clipped `_windowContent` area. Set the
`title` data property in JSON; it defaults to `"(not set)"` when omitted.

```
{
    $controller: "Window",
    $namespace: "MyApp",
    $use: ["ZurfurGui.Windows"],
    title: "Settings",
    $content: [
        {
            $controller: "Panel",
            $layout: "Column",
            $content: [
                { $controller: "TextView", text: "Settings content" }
            ]
        }
    ]
}
```

For a standard floating window, use `AppWindow.ShowWindow` to wrap a control in a `Window` and set its
title from C#:

```csharp
app.ShowWindow(new SettingsView(), "Settings", location: new PointProp(24, 32));
```

The optional `location` sets the window's `Panel.Offset`. Dragging the window updates the same position. Use
`$visualOffset` to move a view without changing the measured content extent.

The window content area clips overflow but does not scroll automatically. Put a `ScrollViewer` in the
content when the window body needs to scroll. The title bar remains outside that content area.

### TextView

`TextView` displays text. Its `text` property can be a string or an array of lines. Use styles and layout
properties to control its appearance and position.

```
{
    $controller: "TextView",
    text: "Hello"
}
```

### Button

`Button` displays a clickable button. Set its `text` property in ZUI. Give it a `$name` when application
code needs to access it from the generated controller.

```
{
    $name: "buttonSave",
    $controller: "Button",
    text: "Save"
}
```

Subscribe to the button's `Click` event in the view's `.Control.cs` partial class. Use the public
`Click` event instead of low-level pointer events:

```csharp
public partial class MainView
{
    public MainView()
    {
        InitializeControl();
        buttonSave.Click += ButtonSave_Click;
    }

    private void ButtonSave_Click(object? sender, EventArgs e)
    {
        // Execute the save operation.
    }
}
```

### Scrim

`Scrim` displays a themed, full-screen overlay for transient UI such as dropdowns, menus, and modal
content. Its background uses the active theme's `color.surface.overlay.scrim` token.

Call `Show` with the current `AppWindow` to display the Scrim. It returns the `View` added to the
floating-window layer. Subscribe to `Dismissed` to close the transient UI, then remove the returned view
from its parent:

```csharp
View? scrimView = null;
var scrim = new Scrim();
scrim.Dismissed += (_, _) => scrimView?.RemoveFromParent();
scrimView = scrim.Show(appWindow);
```

The caller owns the Scrim's lifetime. Remove its returned view when the transient UI closes. Also remove
it when the owning control is detached. Content displayed above the Scrim should be added as a separate
floating panel rather than as a child of the Scrim, so clicks on that content do not dismiss the Scrim.

### ScrollBar

`ScrollBar` displays and changes a numeric scroll value between its `minimum` and `maximum` values. Its
`value` property is data, so application code can read or change it through the generated `DataContext`.

Scrollbars are commonly managed by `ScrollViewer` rather than created directly. Direct scrollbar usage
is useful when an application needs to provide its own scrolling behavior. Set `expandOnHover` to
`true` to use the compact appearance until the scrollbar is hovered, pressed, or dragged. For automatic
scrollbar behavior, see [ScrollViewer](scroll-viewer.md).

### ScrollViewer

`ScrollViewer` displays content through a clipped viewport and provides horizontal and vertical
scrolling. Put the content to scroll in its `$content` section. The combined visible offset is available
through `ScrollOffset`.

For layout, scrolling, scrollbar visibility, range behavior, and detailed usage, see
[ScrollViewer](scroll-viewer.md).

### ListBox

`ListBox<Item>` displays a vertically scrolling list with optional single or multiple selection. Its
items are data objects, and `SelectionChanged` reports changes to the selected items. For item types,
selection APIs, runtime collection updates, and custom items, see [ListBox](list-box.md).

### ComboBox

`ComboBox<Item>` displays a single-selection dropdown. Populate its generated `DataContext.Items`
collection with item data objects and set `DataContext.SelectedIndex` to select an item.

For population, selection, and custom item renderers, see [ComboBox](combo-box.md).

### TreeView

`TreeView<Item>` displays a vertically scrolling tree with optional single or multiple selection.
For item types, selection APIs, runtime collection updates, and custom items, see [ListBox](list-box.md).

================================================================================
FILE: docs/input-events.md
================================================================================
# Input and pointer events

## Overview

This document describes the current high-level path for mouse and pointer input through ZurfurGui. It
starts after platform or browser input has been received; operating-system input processing is outside
the GUI layer.

The main processing phases are:

1. **Find the hit target and build the view chain.** Hit testing identifies the target and its ancestors,
   unless the contact is captured.
2. **Preview routing.** Uncaptured pointer events travel from the root toward the hit target.
3. **Bubble routing.** Uncaptured pointer events travel from the hit target back toward the root unless
   preview handling stopped the route.
4. **Action and state updates.** The system completes gestures and updates hover, pressed, and capture
   state, including cleanup on release or cancellation.

## Public API and behavior

### Common pointer events

| Event | Delivery | When it is raised |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `PreviewPointerDown` | Routed, root to target | A pointer-down input is processed. |
| `PointerDown` | Routed, target to root | After preview unless handled or cancelled. |
| `PreviewPointerMove` | Routed, root to target | A pointer-move input is processed. |
| `PointerMove` | Routed, target to root | After preview unless handled or cancelled. |
| `PreviewPointerUp` | Routed, root to target | A pointer-up input is processed. |
| `PointerUp` | Routed, target to root | After preview unless handled or cancelled. |
| `PointerEntered` | Direct to each entering view | Its per-contact hover-chain membership begins. |
| `PointerExited` | Direct to each exiting view | Its per-contact hover-chain membership ends. |
| `PointerCaptureLost` | Direct to affected views | Capture ends or a gesture cancels their press; carries the contact key. |

For down, move, and up, the hit chain is used unless the contact is captured; then only its capture owner
receives the event. Captured contacts are still hit-tested for hover. Enter and exit are not routed or
redirected by capture.

`Panel.PointerEntered` and `Panel.PointerExited` are direct per-view notifications, not preview/bubble
routed events. They are raised when the router updates the hover chain and finds changed membership.
This normally occurs when the hit view changes; down and up also refresh the chain:

- A view receives `PointerEntered` when it joins that contact's hover chain. Entries are notified from ancestor to target.
- A view receives `PointerExited` when it leaves that contact's hover chain. Exits are notified from target to ancestor.
- Views shared by the old and new chains receive neither notification.
- The event's `Kind` is `Enter` or `Leave`, respectively. Both carry the `PointerContact` from the
  input that caused the chain change.
- The contact includes device, ID, position, dimensions, buttons, and modifiers. On platform leave, position fields
  may be outside the canvas or unsuitable as an in-view position.
- These notifications are independent of capture. A captured contact still updates its hit-tested hover chain.
- Platform enter can cause control enters if the hover chain gains views. Platform leave exits the
  chain's current members.
- The router updates hover state and `IsPointerOver` before invoking enter/exit handlers.

Register handlers with `View.AddEvent(Panel.PointerEntered, handler)` and
`View.AddEvent(Panel.PointerExited, handler)`. These direct notifications do not use `Handled` to stop
other views from being notified. `Handled` and `Cancelled` affect routed down, move, and up dispatch;
they do not undo a hover-chain change that has already been applied.

### Pointer state and capture

The router tracks the current hover target independently from pointer capture:

- `IsPointerOver` is true when at least one tracked contact's hover chain contains the view, unless any
  mouse button is down or a touch contact is active. In those cases it is false for every view.
- `IsPressed` represents the active press relationship.
- Capture lets a control continue receiving pointer events after the pointer leaves its normal bounds.

Each contact has independent hover, press, and capture state, with at most one capture owner. An
uncaptured event routes through its current hit chain. When capture is active, only the owner receives
the event; it is not also sent through the current hit chain. A new capture request replaces the previous
owner and raises `PointerCaptureLost` on that view. The previous press is cancelled, preventing affected
views from remaining pressed or activating on pointer-up; `PointerCaptureLost` is also raised on those
views, except the new capture owner. The normal hit test still runs, but `IsPointerOver` remains false
while any mouse button is down or a touch contact is active.

While capture is active:

- Down, move, and up events are routed only to the capture owner. Ancestors are not added automatically.
- The owner receives pointer-up even if the pointer has moved outside its bounds.
- A pointer leave changes hover state but does not release capture.
- A platform pointer cancel uses the capture/press cleanup path, not normal preview/bubble routing. The
  capture owner receives `PointerCaptureLost`, and the contact's hover and state are removed.

Without capture, `IsPressed` is true only for views shared by the current hover chain and the press chain
recorded on pointer-down. It clears for a view when the pointer leaves that chain and becomes true again
if the pointer returns while the press is still active. The capture owner remains pressed while capture
is active, even outside that chain.

Controls that start a drag or similar interaction generally capture during pointer-down and use capture
loss to clean up. This is important because a release can occur outside the original target, and capture
can end without a normal pointer-up reaching that control.

Gesture recognizers observe contacts alongside raw pointer routing. Pending recognition is not capture;
an accepted recognizer can receive exclusive logical capture. See
[Gesture Recognizers](gesture-recognizer.md) for the arena and recognizer behavior.

Hover and pressed pseudo-properties are updated as chains and capture state change. This allows styles
and controls to react to pointer state without requiring every control to maintain its own hover
bookkeeping.

### Using pointer capture

Pointer capture is for controls that must continue an interaction after the pointer leaves their normal
hit area. Typical examples are dragging a thumb, resizing a window, or implementing a gesture. A
control requests capture by calling its view's `SetCapture` method during its `PointerDown` handler,
passing the contact key:

```csharp
void OnPointerDown(object? sender, PointerEvent e)
{
    View.SetCapture(e.Contact.Key, true);
}
```

Release capture explicitly with `SetCapture` when the interaction ends early:

```csharp
View.SetCapture(e.Contact.Key, false);
```

Controls that capture should also handle `Panel.PointerCaptureLost`. Capture can end without a normal
pointer-up, for example when a contact is cancelled or another control takes over capture. View removal
currently requires the control's own detach cleanup; automatic router cleanup is future work. Use the
handler to clear drag and pressed state, and make the cleanup safe to run more than once:

```csharp
View.AddEvent(Panel.PointerCaptureLost, OnPointerCaptureLost);

void OnPointerCaptureLost(object? sender, PointerContactKey contactKey)
{
    isDragging = false;
    View.SetProperty(Panel.IsPressed, false);
}
```

When adding or changing a captured interaction, verify these transitions: press inside and release
inside, press and drag outside before release, pointer leave while captured, and capture loss without a
normal pointer-up event.

Capture is contact-aware: use `e.Contact.Key` to identify the contact. Setting capture for a key that is
not currently tracked throws; releasing an untracked key is a no-op. `ClearCaptures()` releases all
contacts owned by that view. Capture is not a general-purpose way to make a button clickable. Buttons
should normally use the higher-level `Click` event. Capture keeps low-level pointer events together for
an interaction, but it does not by itself make a click valid when the pointer is released outside the
original press target.

### Clicks and gestures

The router does not synthesize a generic click event. Controls use `ClickRecognizer` or another gesture
recognizer for higher-level actions. See [Gesture Recognizers](gesture-recognizer.md) for click, long-click,
pan, and custom recognizer behavior.

### Wheel events

Mouse wheel input is separate from pointer events. It does not use capture, hover, press, or the gesture
arena, and has no preview or bubble phase.

Views can handle wheel input with `Panel.PointerWheel`. If a handler leaves `WheelEvent.Handled` false,
the event continues toward parent views. `ScrollViewer` sets `Handled` whenever it can scroll in the
wheel's direction (even at the end of its range), so a wheel only reaches a parent scroller when the
child cannot scroll that way.

Deltas use the browser's pixel-mode convention. One detent of a typical mouse wheel is 100 units
(`WheelEvent.UnitsPerNotch`), positive `DeltaY` scrolls down, and positive `DeltaX` scrolls right.

### Timestamps

`PointerEvent.Timestamp` is the event time in milliseconds from a monotonic clock. Only differences
between events of one contact are meaningful. Recognizers use it to measure velocity.

================================================================================
# Gesture recognizers

## Overview

Gesture recognizers turn pointer input into higher-level interactions such as clicks and pans. A
recognizer can accept or reject an interaction, allowing controls to compose gestures such as a button
inside a scrolling list. The current system supports one pointer contact per gesture.

## Public API

### `IGestureRecognizer` and `IGestureRecognizerSession`

Implement `IGestureRecognizer` to provide a gesture attached to a view. Its `CreateSession` method
receives a `GestureSessionContext` and returns independent state for that recognizer/contact candidate.
Implement `IGestureRecognizerSession` for that contact-specific state and respond to the pointer-down,
move, up, and cancellation callbacks. The session interface does not expose a view; use the context's
`CandidateView` for the candidate view.

Attach a recognizer with `View.AddGestureRecognizer`, which returns the recognizer, and detach it with
`View.RemoveGestureRecognizer`. A recognizer is considered for every contact whose hit path includes a
view it is attached to. Removing a recognizer cancels its live sessions: a pending session is rejected,
and a winner cancels the arena and releases its capture. The exception is a winner that is receiving
pointer-up, such as a click handler that removes its own recognizer; it is already completing normally.
Recognizers own nothing that needs disposal, so `IGestureRecognizer` is not `IDisposable`. A
recognizer and its view normally share a lifetime, so detaching is only needed to stop recognition early.

### Attached and candidate views

The attached view is the view a recognizer was added to. The recognizer does not know it. The candidate
view is the view associated with one recognizer/contact attempt and is exposed as
`GestureSessionContext.CandidateView`. They are the same view; a recognizer instance added to more than
one view gets a separate candidate for each participating view. If a session accepts before pointer-up,
its candidate view receives the capture.

The arena gives each candidate a `GestureSessionContext` with the `CandidateView`, the initial `Contact`
snapshot, the derived `ContactKey`, and the `Accept()` and `Reject()` operations. The context becomes
inactive when the session completes or is canceled, so later calls have no effect. It can be used from
a timer callback while the contact is active. Later pointer updates arrive as the `PointerEvent` copies
passed to the session (kind, contact, and cancellation flag; `Handled` is independent of raw routed
events).

A custom recognizer can use this general shape:

```csharp
sealed class ExampleRecognizer : IGestureRecognizer
{
    public IGestureRecognizerSession? CreateSession(GestureSessionContext context) =>
        new ExampleSession(context);
}

// Attach: view.AddGestureRecognizer(new ExampleRecognizer());

sealed class ExampleSession : IGestureRecognizerSession
{
    readonly GestureSessionContext _context;

    public ExampleSession(GestureSessionContext context)
    {
        _context = context;
    }

    public void OnPointerDown(PointerEvent e) { }
    public void OnPointerMove(PointerEvent e) { }

    public void OnPointerUp(PointerEvent e)
    {
        if (/* this interaction matched */)
            _context.Accept();
        else
            _context.Reject();
    }

    public void OnCancelled() { }
}
```

Use `_context.CandidateView` to access the candidate view and `_context.Contact` for the initial
contact snapshot.

### `ClickRecognizer`

`ClickRecognizer` is the first concrete `IGestureRecognizer`. It is used by `Button`, `ComboBox`,
`Scrim`, and other controls. Construct it with the callback and add it to the view that owns the
interaction. The view owns the recognizer, so the control does not keep a reference or remove it when it
detaches; a control that is moved to a new parent keeps working:

```csharp
public ExampleControl()
{
    InitializeControl();
    View.AddGestureRecognizer(new ClickRecognizer(OnClick));
}

void OnClick(object? sender, PointerEvent e)
{
    // Perform the control action.
}
```

A click is accepted on pointer-up if the contact is not canceled and its device position is inside the
attached view's `OriginRect`. It remains a candidate while down; it does not capture or mark raw pointer
events handled while pending. Thus raw pointer handlers, including handlers on ancestors, continue to
receive events unless they handle them or request direct capture. A click callback runs after the raw
pointer-up route for that input.

By default a mouse click requires the left button. Pass a `mouseButtons` argument to change it, for
example `new ClickRecognizer(OnClick, null, PointerButtons.Right)`, or `PointerButtons.None` to prevent
the mouse from clicking. A mouse button that does not match never becomes a candidate. Touch and pen
are not affected.

The optional long-click callback uses `AppWindow.Properties.LongClickDuration` and
`LongClickMovementTolerance`. Moving farther than the tolerance stops long-click eligibility but does
not by itself reject the ordinary click. If the long-click callback sets
`PointerLongClickEventArgs.Handled`, the session accepts and captures its view and suppresses the click
on release. If the callback calls `SetCapture` on another view, that direct capture preempts the arena
and cancels the click session.

### `PanRecognizer`

`PanRecognizer` recognizes dragging after the contact moves past its slop. It reports movement and release
velocity; the owner applies movement and, if desired, animates a flick. `ScrollViewer` is an example
([details](scroll-viewer.md)).

```csharp
var pan = view.AddGestureRecognizer(new PanRecognizer());
pan.PanMoved += (s, e) => content.Offset += e.Delta;       // Device pixels
pan.PanEnded += (s, e) => StartMyFlick(e.Velocity);        // Zero unless a touch/pen flicked
```

The session stays pending until the contact moves farther than the slop from the down point along an
enabled axis, then accepts, which cancels competing candidates (such as a child's click) and captures the
contact. A release before that rejects, so a click can still win.

- `PanStarted` reports `SlopDelta`, the movement from the down point to where the pan started. Later
  movement arrives in `PanMoved` as `Delta`, relative to the pan start. Distances are device pixels
  except slop, which is in layout units scaled by the DPR.
- `PanEnded` reports the release `Velocity` (device pixels per second), or `Cancelled`. Velocity is
  zero for a contact that was stationary before release, for the mouse, when `Flick` is off, or below
  `MinFlickVelocity`, and is limited to `MaxFlickVelocity`.
- `PanOptions`: `Axes`, `Slop` (null uses the app window's per-device movement slop; zero or one pans
  almost immediately), `TouchPans`, `PenPans`, `MouseButtons` (default right button), `Flick`,
  `MinFlickVelocity`, `MaxFlickVelocity`.
- With `Axes` of `None` the recognizer creates no session, so an ancestor can pan. Being at the owner's
  scroll limit does not matter to the recognizer.
- `CatchOnDown` lets the owner say that earlier motion (a flick) is still running. The pan then accepts
  immediately on pointer-down, so the touch stops the motion and does not also click.

# ScrollViewer

## Overview

`ScrollViewer` displays content through a clipped viewport and allows the user or application code to
change the visible offset with horizontal and vertical scrollbars.

The current implementation is an early control. It supports the core content, measurement, clipping,
offset, and scrollbar-range behavior, but several standard GUI features remain unfinished.

## How to use ScrollViewer

A ScrollViewer is a container control. Put the content to be scrolled in its `$content` section, just
as content is supplied to a `Panel` or another container control.

```
{
    $controller: "ScrollViewer",
    $content: [
        {
            $controller: "Panel",
            $content: [
                {
                    $controller: "TextView",
                    text: "Scrollable content"
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}
```

The ScrollViewer should normally receive its size from its parent layout. The scrollable content should
not normally have a `$sizeRequest`, because its natural measured size is used to calculate the scroll
range.

A parent layout must provide a finite viewport when the application needs a bounded scrolling area. For
example, a dock layout can place a toolbar at the top and make the final ScrollViewer child fill the
remaining area:

```
{
    $controller: "Panel",
    $layout: "Dock",
    $content: [
        {
            $layout: "Row",
            dock.align: "top",
            $content: [
                {
                    $controller: "TextView",
                    text: "Toolbar"
                }
            ]
        },
        {
            $controller: "ScrollViewer",
            $content: [
                {
                    $controller: "Panel",
                    $content: [
                        // Content that may be larger than the viewport.
                    ]
                }
            ]
        }
    ]
}
```

The final visible child of the current `Dock` layout receives the remaining space. The ScrollViewer
should therefore be the last child when it is intended to fill the area below a top row.

## Public control access

The generated ScrollViewer controller exposes the named scrollbar controls:

```csharp
public ScrollBar horizontalScrollBar;
public ScrollBar verticalScrollBar;
```

It also exposes the combined offset:

```csharp
public Point ScrollOffset { get; set; }
```

The offset is expressed in content coordinates. Increasing `X` moves the content left, and increasing
`Y` moves the content up, revealing content farther to the right or below the viewport.

For example:

```csharp
var offset = scrollViewer.ScrollOffset;
scrollViewer.ScrollOffset = new Point(offset.X, offset.Y + 8);
```

The setter clamps both coordinates to the current scrollbar ranges. Setting an offset outside the valid
range does not throw; it is normalized to the nearest valid value.

Changing a scrollbar's `DataContext.Value` has the same effect:

```csharp
scrollViewer.verticalScrollBar.DataContext.Value += 8;
```

Scrollbar values and `ScrollOffset` are synchronized in both directions.

## Scrollbar data and visibility

Each scrollbar has the following range-related data:

| Property | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `minimum` | The minimum offset, normally `0`. |
| `maximum` | The largest valid offset, calculated as content extent minus viewport extent. |
| `value` | The current offset along the scrollbar's orientation. |
| `viewportSize` | The visible size used to calculate the thumb size. |
| `smallChange` | The small movement amount; the default is currently `0` unless configured. |
| `largeChange` | The page movement amount; the viewer sets it to the viewport size. |
| `visibility` | Whether the viewer displays the scrollbar automatically, always, or never. |

`visibility` uses `ScrollBarVisibility`; its default is `Auto`. The overlay section below describes how
each visibility setting affects rendering.

- `Visible` always displays the scrollbar.
- `Hidden` does not display the scrollbar, but the range and value can still be used programmatically.
- `Auto` displays the scrollbar only when its calculated maximum is greater than its minimum.

## Overlay scrollbar behavior

ScrollViewer uses overlay scrollbars. The scrollbars are drawn above the clipped content and do not
consume viewport space. Showing or hiding either scrollbar therefore does not change the content width,
content height, or the content extent used to calculate the scroll range.

When only one scrollbar is visible, it uses the full corresponding edge of the viewport. When both are
visible, the horizontal scrollbar is shortened by the vertical scrollbar's thickness and the vertical
scrollbar is shortened by the horizontal scrollbar's thickness. This leaves an empty, non-scrollable
corner where the two bars meet. No corner control or gutter is added yet.

`Auto` hides a bar with no scrollable range, `Visible` keeps it rendered, and `Hidden` suppresses it
without removing its range or value.

Scrollbar visibility is evaluated from the content extent and the unchanged viewport size. The
appearance of a scrollbar does not reduce the size used to measure content, so visibility does not
require the iterative two-axis measurement used by traditional scrollbars that consume layout space.

The standard range model is:

```plaintext
Minimum = 0
Maximum = max(0, contentExtent - viewportExtent)
Value   = clamped current offset
```

When content fits in an axis, that axis has a maximum of zero and no scrollable thumb is rendered.

## Mouse wheel

ScrollViewer handles the mouse wheel. It moves the content by `wheelSteps` scroll steps for each wheel
detent. One step is `scrollSize` (16 pixels by default), so the default is 3 x 16 = 48 pixels per
detent.
Fractional wheel deltas from precision touchpads scroll proportionally.

`wheelSteps` is a styled property. It comes from the `scroll.wheel.steps` variable in the base theme
(`ZurfurBase`, default 3) and can be overridden on an individual ScrollViewer:

```
{
	$controller: "ScrollViewer",
	wheelSteps: 5
}
```

- Wheel over any part of the ScrollViewer works, including its content, empty space, and its
  scrollbars.
- Shift+wheel scrolls horizontally when the device reports only vertical movement.
- Horizontal wheel events scroll horizontally.
- Ctrl is ignored by the ScrollViewer. The browser and the WinForms form use Ctrl+wheel for
  magnification, so the platform adapters do not forward it.
- An axis disabled by `scrollMode` ignores its wheel movement.
- The offset is clamped like any other `ScrollOffset` change.
- The ScrollViewer sets `Handled` whenever it can scroll in the wheel's direction according to
  `scrollMode`, even at the end of its range, so a ScrollViewer inside another ScrollViewer does not let
  the parent see that wheel. If it cannot scroll in the wheel's direction (for example a vertical wheel
  over a horizontal-only viewer), it leaves the event unhandled so a parent can scroll. Ctrl is always
  marked handled. Controls inside the viewer can handle the wheel first by setting `Handled` themselves.

Wheel deltas follow the browser's pixel-mode convention: one detent is 100 units, positive Y scrolls
down and positive X scrolls right. Scrolling is therefore `notches * wheelSteps * scrollSize`, added to
`ScrollOffset`.

## Panning and flick

- Touch and pen pan with any contact. The mouse pans only with the right button by default.
- Panning moves `ScrollOffset`, clamped to the scrollbar ranges. The content does not jump when the pan
  starts; the slop distance is ignored.
- On release, a touch or pen contact flicks: the content keeps moving and slows down. The mouse never
  flicks. The viewer stops the flick at the scroll limit on each axis, and touching the viewer during a
  flick stops it without clicking the content under the finger. The wheel, scrollbar changes, and a new
  pan also stop it.
- The viewer pans only on axes it can scroll according to `scrollMode`. A viewer that cannot scroll at
  all does not take part, so an ancestor viewer pans instead. A viewer that can scroll an axis takes the
  pan when movement along that axis passes the slop, even when it is at its limit.

Configure it through `ScrollViewer.PanOptions`:

```csharp
scrollViewer.PanOptions.Slop = 1;                              // Pan almost immediately
scrollViewer.PanOptions.MouseButtons = PointerButtons.Left;    // Left button pans with the mouse
scrollViewer.PanOptions.Flick = false;                         // Stop when released
```

`Slop` is in layout units (scaled by the DPR) and defaults to the app window's movement slop for the
device.

## Sizing and known limitations

The ScrollViewer has no default `$sizeRequest` or `$sizeMax`. Its content is measured separately so it
can be larger than the viewport. The viewer reports the smaller of the content's natural size and the
available parent size.

When content is smaller than the available parent size, the ScrollViewer sizes to the content. When
content is larger, the viewer uses the available size as its finite viewport and scrollbars represent
the overflow. If a parent measures with unconstrained space, the ScrollViewer may grow toward its content
because no finite viewport has been established. Applications should provide a finite constraint
through the viewer's parent when a bounded viewport is required.

Current limitations include:

- No keyboard scrolling.
- No accessibility metadata or automation support.
- No configurable content alignment; content starts at the top-left.
- No configurable scrollbar gutter or overlay inset.
- The overlay corner is currently empty and is not yet represented by a dedicated corner control.
- There are no convenience horizontal/vertical offset or extent/viewport properties.

================================================================================
FILE: docs/list-box.md
================================================================================
# ListBox

## Overview

`ListBox<Item>` is a scrolling, vertical list of items with optional selection. The item controller
is chosen by the item's data type, for example `ListBox<ListBoxItemText>`. Items know nothing about
selection; the list box owns it.

The C# namespace for the control and its marker types is `ZurfurGui.Controls.ListBox`. Add that
namespace to `$use` in the form ZUI that uses the control and the item ZUI that implements
`IListBoxItem`.

## Using it in a ZUI file

```
{
	$name: "_names",
	$controller: "ListBox<ListBoxItemText>",
	$sizeRequest: "width:160,height:300",
	selectionMode: "multiple",
	items: [
		{ text: [ "One" ] },
		{ text: [ "Two" ] }
	]
}
```

- `items` is a list of the item's data class (`ListBoxItemTextData` here).
- `selectionMode` is `none`, `single` (the default), or `multiple`.
- Give the list box a height, otherwise it is as tall as its content.
- Use `SelectionChanged` in code-behind to react to the user:

```csharp
_names.SelectionChanged += (s, e) => Show(_names.SelectedIndices);
```

### Selection API

- `SelectedIndices`: the selected indices in ascending order.
- `SelectedIndex`: the index if exactly one item is selected, otherwise `null`.
- `SelectionChanged`: raised when the set of selected items changes (user input, code, or removal
  of a selected item). It is not raised when an index only shifts because of an add or remove
  elsewhere.
- `Select(index)`, `SetSelectedIndices(indices)`, `ClearSelection()`: change the selection from code.
- `SelectNearest(index)`: selects `index` clamped to the last item, or clears if the list is empty.
  Call it from `SelectionChanged` to select the neighbor of a removed item.

User input: clicking the sole selected item clears the selection in either selection mode. Otherwise,
a click selects that item. In `multiple` mode Ctrl+click and touch click toggle an item, while
Shift+click selects the range from the last item clicked without Shift. There is no keyboard support
yet.
Initial selection cannot be set in a `.zui` file; use `Select` or `SetSelectedIndices` in code.

## Adding and removing items at runtime

`DataContext.Items` is an `ObservableCollection`. Change it and the list box updates:

```csharp
_names.DataContext.Items.Add(new ListBoxItemTextData() { Text = new TextLines("Three") });
_names.DataContext.Items.Insert(0, new ListBoxItemTextData() { Text = new TextLines("Zero") });
_names.DataContext.Items.RemoveAt(2);
```

Selection follows the items. Inserting at or before a selected item shifts its index up, and
removing before it shifts it down. Removing a selected item deselects it (no neighbor is selected
automatically) and raises `SelectionChanged`. Clearing the collection deselects everything.
Assigning a new `Items` collection also clears the selection. To delete the selected items, remove
from the highest index down:

```csharp
foreach (var index in _names.SelectedIndices.Reverse().ToList())
	_names.DataContext.Items.RemoveAt(index);
```

## Creating your own list box items

An item is a normal ZUI view that declares `$implements: "IListBoxItem"`. Its generated data class
then implements `IListBoxItem`, and `ListBox<MyItem>` works. Do not set a background on the item,
because the row behind it draws the hover and selected colors. See
`samples/TestApp/TestApp/Controls/ListBoxItemBadge.zui`.

```
{
	$controller: "ListBoxItemBadge",
	$namespace: "TestApp.Test.Controls",
	$use: ["ZurfurGui.Controls.ListBox"],
	$implements: "IListBoxItem",
	$data: {
		text: { type: "TextLines", bind: "data:_text.text" }
	},
	$content: [ { $name: "_text", $controller: "TextView" } ]
}
```

Use it with `$controller: "ListBox<ListBoxItemBadge>"`, and add `$use` for the item's namespace in
the form's ZUI file when it is not the same namespace.

Not implemented yet: keyboard input, focus, virtualization, fixed row heights, and diffing.

================================================================================
FILE: docs/combo-box.md
================================================================================
# ComboBox

## Overview

`ComboBox<Item>` is a generic single-selection dropdown control. In ZUI, `Item` is written as the item
controller name, but generated C# closes the generic controller with that control's concrete data class.
The item data class contains the data needed by its renderer; selection state belongs to the combo box
rather than individual items.

The C# namespace for these types is `ZurfurGui.Controls.ComboBox`. A view that uses the control
should include that namespace in its `$use` list.

## Using ComboBox in a view

Because `ComboBox` is generic, use the item controller name in a concrete closed form in `.zui`:

```
{
    $name: "_themeComboBox",
    $controller: "ComboBox<ComboBoxItemText>",
    $align: { horizontal: "left" }
}
```

The item data class must implement `IComboBoxItem`. An item view normally declares this with
`$implements: "IComboBoxItem"` in its ZUI definition.

## Populating and using ComboBox from code

Add data objects, not item controllers, to the collection:

```csharp
foreach (var label in new[] { "Zurfur Light", "Zurfur Dark", "Cherry Light", "Cherry Dark" })
{
    _themeComboBox.DataContext.Items.Add(new ComboBoxItemTextData { Text = new TextLines(label) });
}
_themeComboBox.DataContext.SelectedIndex = 0;
```

`Items` is a live `ObservableCollection<T>`.

### Reacting to selection changes

Subscribe to `DataContext.PropertyChanged` and check for `SelectedIndex`:

```csharp
_themeComboBox.DataContext.PropertyChanged += (s, e) =>
{
    if (e.PropertyName != "SelectedIndex")
        return;
    var idx = _themeComboBox.DataContext.SelectedIndex;
    // idx is int? -- null means no selection
};
```

`SelectedIndex` is `null` when nothing is selected. Set it programmatically to change the displayed
item:

```csharp
_themeComboBox.DataContext.SelectedIndex = 2;
```

## Adding a ComboBox item renderer

A new item renderer declares its own view-shaped data. If the item is used with `ComboBox`, its ZUI
definition declares `$implements: "IComboBoxItem"`.

For example, `ComboBoxItemBadge.zui` declares `Badge` and `Text` data:

```
{
    $controller: "ComboBoxItemBadge",
    $namespace: "TestApp.Test.Controls",
    $use: ["ZurfurGui.Controls.ComboBox"],
    $implements: "IComboBoxItem",
    $data: {
        badge: {
            type: "TextLines",
            bind: "_badge.text"
        },
        text: {
            type: "TextLines",
            bind: "_text.text"
        }
    },
    $layout: "Row"
}
```

Use the item in a view with the controller name, not the generated data class name:

```
{
    $name: "_badgeCombo",
    $controller: "ComboBox<ComboBoxItemBadge>",
    $align: { horizontal: "left" }
}
```

Populate it with the concrete generated data class:

```csharp
_badgeCombo.DataContext.Items.Add(new ComboBoxItemBadgeData
{
    Badge = new("A"),
    Text = new("Pick 1")
});
```

`IsSelected` is not an item property. Selection is owned by `ComboBoxData<TItem>.SelectedIndex`. Items
also do not receive common `IsEnabled` or `Tag` properties automatically; add such properties to the
item's own data shape only when the application requires them.

================================================================================
FILE: docs/tree-view.md
================================================================================
# TreeView

## Overview

`TreeView<Item>` shows a scrolling tree of nodes. Each node has text (and optionally an icon or other
content), can have child nodes, and can be expanded, collapsed, and selected. The node controller is
chosen by the concrete node data type, for example `TreeView<TreeNodeText>`.

The tree draws the connecting lines and the expander (a box with `+` and `-`, or a chevron) itself.
Selection and expansion are plain flags in the node data, so the app can read and change them
without calling the tree.

The files are in `src/ZurfurGui/Controls/TreeView`, in the `ZurfurGui.Controls.TreeView` namespace.
The test form is `FormTestTreeView` in the test app.

| File | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `TreeView.zui`, `TreeView.Control.cs` | The tree control. |
| `TreeNode.cs` | The `ITreeNode<TSelf>` data contract every node must satisfy. |
| `TreeNodeText.zui` | The built-in node: an optional icon and text. |
| `TreeNodeView.zui` | Internal. One node: a header row above a stack of child nodes. |
| `TreeNodeRow.zui` | Internal. The header, which draws the hover and selected background. |
| `TreeGutter.zui`, `TreeGutter.Control.cs` | Internal. Draws the lines and the expander. |

## Using the tree

### Building the data

Add root nodes to `DataContext.Items` and child nodes to each node's `Children`:

```csharp
var node = new TreeNodeTextData() { Text = new TextLines("Parent"), IsExpanded = true };
node.Children.Add(new TreeNodeTextData() { Text = new TextLines("Child") });
tree.DataContext.Items.Add(node);
```

The collections are `ObservableCollection`, so the tree updates when nodes are added, removed,
replaced, moved, or cleared at any depth.

### Declaring the tree in a `.zui` file

Include `ZurfurGui.Controls.TreeView` and `ZurfurGui.Controls.ListBox` in the form's `$use` list.
The tree namespace provides the control and node contract; the list-box namespace provides the
shared `SelectionMode` enum.

```
{ $controller: "TreeView<TreeNodeText>", selectionMode: "single", showLines: false }
```

`selectionMode` is data. The other settings are styles, so a theme can change them for every tree,
and a value in the `.zui` file or in code applies to that one tree only. The defaults are theme
variables in `ZurfurBase.zth`.

| Setting | Theme variable | Default | Meaning |
|---------|----------------|---------|---------|
| `selectionMode` | (data) | single | `none`, `single`, or `multiple`. |
| `showLines` | `treeview.show-lines` | true | Draw the lines connecting nodes. |
| `showExpander` | `treeview.show-expander` | true | Draw the expander of nodes that have children. |
| `indentWidth` | `treeview.indent-width` | 16 | Width of each depth level. |
| `lineWidth` | `treeview.line-width` | 1 | Thickness of the lines and the expander. |
| `expanderStyle` | `treeview.expander-style` | box | `box` (plus and minus) or `chevron`. |

The lines are always solid. The line color is the theme variable `color.treeview.line`. The row
background is `color.treeview.row.background`, which uses the condition `TreeNodeRow.isSelected`.

### Selecting and expanding

- Click a row to select its node. Click the expander to expand or collapse it. Clicking the
  expander does not change the selection.
- Clicking the sole selected node clears the selection in either selection mode. Otherwise, a row
  click selects that node.
- In `multiple` mode, Ctrl+click and touch click toggle a node, and Shift+click selects the visible
  nodes from the last node clicked without Shift to the clicked node, replacing the selection. Shift
  wins over Ctrl. If the start node is gone or hidden, the selected visible node nearest to the click
  is the start. Nodes inside collapsed branches are skipped by the range. A plain click or a Shift
  range also deselects selected nodes that are hidden in collapsed branches. In `single` and `none`
  mode the modifier keys are ignored.
- To change the state from code, write the flag: `node.IsSelected = true` or
  `node.IsExpanded = false`. There is no `Select` or `Expand` method. The tree writes the same
  flags when the user clicks.
- `SelectedNodes` walks the data and returns every node whose flag is set, in tree order,
  including nodes in collapsed branches. It is lazy, so flags may be changed while enumerating, and
  it works while the tree is detached.
- `ClearSelection()` deselects every node and `SelectAll()` selects every node (only in `multiple`
  mode, while attached). Each raises `SelectionChanged` once.
- `SelectionChanged` is raised when the selected set changes. It has no arguments, so read the
  data. It is raised for user input, for flag changes made by app code, when a flagged node is
  added, and when a selected node is removed. A click, `ClearSelection`, and `SelectAll` raise it
  once however many flags they write, but flags written by app code raise it once per flag.
- Selecting a node does not expand its ancestors or scroll to it. An app that wants the selected
  node to be visible sets `IsExpanded` on the ancestors itself.
- Collapsing a parent of the selected node leaves the selection on the hidden node.
- Removing the selected node de-selects it. No neighbor is selected. An app that wants one can
  select it in `SelectionChanged`.

### Creating your own tree nodes

Copy this `.zui` and change the names and the content. The test app has a complete example in
`Controls/TreeNodeBadge.zui`.

```
{
    $controller: "MyNode",
    $namespace: "MyApp",
    $use: ["ZurfurGui.Controls.TreeView"],
    $implements: "ITreeNode<MyNodeData>",
    $data: {
        children: { type: "[]MyNode", bind: "data" },
        isExpanded: { type: "Bool", bind: "data" },
        isSelected: { type: "Bool", bind: "data" },
        text: { type: "TextLines", bind: "data:_text.text" }
    },
    $content: [
        { $name: "_text", $controller: "TextView" }
    ]
}
```

Rules:

- `$implements` is `ITreeNode<` plus the node's own data class name (the controller name plus
  `Data`), for example `ITreeNode<MyNodeData>`.
- `$data` must declare `children` as `[]` plus the node's own controller name, and `isExpanded` and
  `isSelected` as bools, all with `bind: "data"`.
- Add `$use` for the node's namespace in the form's `.zui` when it differs.
- Use it as `TreeView<MyNode>`.
- A missing member or a misspelled name shows up as an ordinary C# error that the interface is not
  implemented.
- Do not set a background on the node, because the row draws the hover and selected colors.
- A node object must appear once, in one tree, and the data must not contain cycles. These are not
  detected.
